_README: Procedure-specific patient-education content. One key per 'specialty/slug'. Every entry must be signed off by a qualified clinician before the page is indexed; set reviewedBy/reviewedOn when that happens. Ranges are general patient-education figures, not a promise about any individual case.

what: A dental implant is a small titanium or zirconia post placed into the jawbone to replace the root of a missing tooth. Once the bone has healed around the post — a process called osseointegration — an abutment and a crown, bridge or denture are attached on top. The implant itself is never visible; what you see is the restoration fixed to it.

Treatment normally runs in two stages. The implant is placed under local anaesthetic in a visit of roughly one to two hours, then left to integrate for around three to six months before the final restoration is fitted. Some cases allow a temporary tooth on the day of surgery, and a smaller number allow immediate loading with the definitive restoration, but whether that is possible depends on bone quality and bite forces rather than on preference.
dental/dental-implants.why: Implants are usually considered when one or more teeth are missing or failing and a patient wants a fixed replacement that does not rely on grinding down neighbouring teeth, as a conventional bridge does. They also stimulate the jawbone in a way that dentures do not, which slows the bone resorption that follows tooth loss.
suitable: Adults with completed jaw growth and one or more missing or unrestorable teeth
Sufficient bone volume and density, or willingness to undergo grafting or a sinus lift first
Healthy gums, with any active periodontal disease treated beforehand
Able to maintain thorough daily cleaning around the implant
notsuitable: Active, untreated gum disease or widespread untreated decay
Heavy smoking, which measurably raises the risk of implant failure
Poorly controlled diabetes or conditions that impair bone healing
Certain bone medicines, including some bisphosphonates and denosumab, which need specialist assessment
Untreated severe bruxism without a plan to manage the grinding forces
recovery: First 48 hours: swelling, mild bruising and discomfort managed with simple analgesia; soft diet
First week: sutures often removed around day 7–10; avoid the surgical site when brushing
3–6 months: integration period, usually with a temporary tooth in place if the gap is visible
Second stage: abutment and final restoration fitted, typically over one to two appointments
Long term: professional maintenance every six to twelve months to monitor the tissue around the implant
risks: Failure to integrate, so the implant loosens and has to be removed and replaced
Infection at the surgical site, or peri-implantitis later if cleaning is inadequate
Nerve injury causing numbness or altered sensation in the lip, chin or tongue — uncommon, occasionally lasting
Sinus complications when implants are placed in the upper back jaw
Damage to adjacent teeth or restorations during placement
Mechanical problems over time: screw loosening, crown fracture, chipped porcelain
alternatives: Conventional fixed bridge supported by the neighbouring teeth
Removable partial or full denture
Resin-bonded bridge for a single front tooth
Leaving the gap, where the bite and appearance allow it

glance.Return-travel window: Confirmed by the clinic, often 2–3 days after placement

what: Root canal treatment — endodontic treatment — removes infected or inflamed pulp from inside a tooth. The dentist opens the crown of the tooth, cleans and shapes the narrow canals inside each root, disinfects them, then fills and seals them so bacteria cannot recolonise the space. The aim is to keep a tooth that would otherwise need extraction.

Most treatments are completed in one or two visits of roughly 60 to 90 minutes under local anaesthetic. Molars have more canals than front teeth and take longer. Because the remaining tooth is more brittle once the pulp is gone, a back tooth is usually protected with a crown or onlay afterwards; this second stage is a separate appointment and a separate cost.
dental/root-canal-treatment.why: Patients are usually referred after persistent toothache, prolonged sensitivity to heat or cold, pain on biting, a dental abscess, or an X-ray finding of infection at the root tip. It is also needed when trauma or deep decay has exposed the pulp.
suitable: A tooth with irreversible pulpitis, pulp necrosis or apical infection
Enough sound tooth structure remaining to restore afterwards
Root canals that can be located and negotiated on assessment
Adequate surrounding bone and gum support
notsuitable: A vertical root fracture, which generally makes the tooth unsavable
Severe decay leaving too little tooth to restore
Advanced periodontal disease around the same tooth
Cases better served by extraction and an implant or bridge, on the clinician's assessment
recovery: First 24–48 hours: tenderness on biting is common; over-the-counter analgesia is usually enough
Avoid chewing firmly on the tooth until the permanent restoration is placed
Most people return to normal activity the same or next day
Definitive crown or onlay typically fitted within a few weeks
Follow-up X-ray commonly recommended at 6–12 months to confirm healing
risks: Persistent or recurrent infection requiring retreatment or apical surgery
A canal that cannot be fully cleaned because of curvature, calcification or unusual anatomy
Instrument separation inside a canal
Perforation of the root wall
Fracture of the treated tooth, particularly if the crown is delayed
Post-operative pain lasting longer than expected, sometimes needing a further visit
alternatives: Extraction, followed by an implant, bridge or denture — or by leaving the gap
Pulpotomy or pulp capping in selected cases where the pulp is still vital
Apicoectomy where a previous root canal has failed and retreatment is not viable
Monitoring with no immediate treatment, only where the tooth is symptom-free and the clinician judges it appropriate

glance.Typical procedure time: 60–90 minutes per visit, one or two visits
glance.Restoration: Crown or onlay usually needed on back teeth
glance.Return-travel window: Often the next day, confirmed by the clinic

what: A veneer is a thin shell of porcelain or composite bonded to the front surface of a tooth to change its colour, shape, length or alignment. Porcelain veneers are made in a laboratory and cemented at a second visit; composite veneers are shaped directly on the tooth in a single appointment.

Most porcelain veneers require a small amount of enamel to be removed — commonly around 0.3 to 0.7 mm — so the result sits flush with the neighbouring teeth. That reduction is permanent: once a tooth is prepared for a veneer, it will need a veneer or crown for the rest of its life. Minimal-preparation and no-preparation veneers exist but only suit a narrower set of cases.
dental/dental-veneers.why: Veneers are usually considered for discoloration that does not respond to whitening, chipped or worn edges, small gaps, mildly rotated or uneven teeth, or an overall change in the look of the smile line. They address appearance, not disease.
suitable: Healthy teeth and gums, with decay and gum disease treated first
Enough sound enamel for a reliable bond
A cosmetic concern confined to the visible front teeth
Realistic expectations agreed with the clinician at the planning stage
notsuitable: Active decay, untreated gum disease or root infection
Significant bruxism without a night guard and bite management
Substantial crowding or bite problems better corrected with orthodontics first
Heavily filled or structurally weak teeth, where a crown is the sounder option
recovery: Temporary veneers worn between preparation and fitting, usually one to two weeks
Sensitivity to hot and cold for a few days to a few weeks after preparation
Normal eating usually resumes within 24 hours of final bonding, avoiding very hard foods
A night guard is commonly advised for anyone who grinds
Routine hygiene visits to monitor the margins and gum health
risks: Irreversible enamel removal
Chipping, debonding or fracture, requiring repair or replacement
Ongoing sensitivity
Colour mismatch with surrounding natural teeth, or staining at the margins over time
Gum irritation or recession exposing the veneer edge
Pulp inflammation occasionally requiring root canal treatment later
alternatives: Professional tooth whitening for discoloration alone
Direct composite bonding, which removes little or no enamel and is reversible
Orthodontics or clear aligners for alignment and spacing
Crowns where the tooth is structurally compromised
Enamel reshaping and polishing for very minor irregularities

glance.Typical procedure time: Two visits over roughly a week for porcelain
glance.Return-travel window: After the final fit, confirmed by the clinic

what: Follicular unit excision (FUE) moves hair from the back and sides of the scalp — the donor area, which is genetically resistant to pattern hair loss — to thinning or bald regions. Individual follicular units of one to four hairs are removed one at a time with a punch typically under a millimetre across, then placed into recipient sites in the planned pattern.

A session commonly lasts six to eight hours under local anaesthetic and moves somewhere between 1,500 and 4,000 grafts, depending on donor density and the area being covered. FUE leaves scattered small dot scars across the donor zone rather than the single linear scar of a strip procedure, which is why it suits people who wear their hair short.
hair-restoration/fue-hair-transplant.why: Most patients are men with androgenetic alopecia at a stable stage, but FUE is also used for a receding hairline, thinning crowns, scar coverage and to refine the results of earlier surgery. It redistributes existing hair; it does not create new follicles or stop ongoing loss.
suitable: A pattern of loss that has been stable long enough for a realistic plan to be made
Adequate donor density at the back and sides
Realistic expectations about coverage, given a fixed lifetime donor supply
General health that allows a long procedure under local anaesthetic
notsuitable: Rapidly progressing loss in a young patient, where medical treatment is usually recommended first
Diffuse unpatterned thinning that also affects the donor area
Active scalp disease, or scarring alopecias that are still inflamed
Bleeding disorders or anticoagulation that cannot safely be managed around surgery
Expectations of density matching an unaffected scalp
recovery: Days 1–3: swelling of the forehead is common; the recipient area is crusted and tender
Day 7–10: crusts clear with the washing routine set by the clinic
Weeks 2–6: transplanted hairs shed — this is expected and not a sign of failure
Months 3–4: new growth begins
Months 8–12: most of the result is visible; final density typically judged at 12–18 months
Strenuous exercise, swimming and direct sun are usually restricted for several weeks
risks: Poor graft survival, giving thinner coverage than planned
Visible donor depletion or over-harvesting
Folliculitis or infection in the recipient area
Numbness or altered sensation, usually temporary
Shock loss of existing hairs around the transplanted zone
An unnatural hairline design, which is difficult and sometimes impossible to correct
Continued loss of untransplanted hair, changing the result over time
alternatives: Medical therapy such as topical minoxidil or oral finasteride, on prescription and clinician assessment
DHI, where grafts are implanted with a pen-shaped tool
FUT strip harvesting where very high graft numbers are needed
Scalp micropigmentation for the appearance of density without surgery
Hair systems, or accepting the loss

what: Direct Hair Implantation (DHI) is a variation of FUE. Grafts are harvested the same way, but instead of creating recipient channels first and then placing grafts into them, the surgeon loads each graft into a hollow implanter pen that makes the channel and sets the graft in one movement.

The practical differences are shorter time out of the body for each graft and tighter control over the angle, depth and direction of placement — which is why DHI is often chosen for hairlines and for adding density between existing hairs. It is slower per graft than standard FUE, so sessions may cover a smaller area or run longer.
hair-restoration/dhi-hair-transplant.why: DHI is generally selected for frontal hairline work, for filling in among existing hair where channel creation risks damaging what is already there, and for smaller, detail-driven cases. It is a placement technique, not a different operation, and it does not change what the donor area can supply.
suitable: Hairline design and frontal density work
Adding grafts between existing hairs without transecting them
Small to moderate session sizes
The same stability and donor-supply conditions that apply to any transplant
notsuitable: Very large sessions where standard FUE is usually more efficient
Unstable or diffuse loss involving the donor area
Active scalp disease or inflamed scarring alopecia
Anyone for whom transplantation itself is not yet appropriate
recovery: Recovery follows the same course as FUE
Crusting clears over roughly 7–10 days with the clinic's washing routine
Shedding of transplanted hairs at weeks 2–6 is expected
Growth from around month 3–4; result assessed at 12–18 months
Exercise, swimming and sun exposure restricted for several weeks
risks: The same risk profile as FUE: graft failure, infection, shock loss, numbness, donor depletion
Graft crush or damage if implanter technique is poor
Longer time in the chair for the same graft count
Marketing claims about superiority that outrun the evidence — the surgeon's skill matters more than the tool
alternatives: Standard FUE, which suits larger sessions
FUT strip harvesting for very high graft numbers
Medical therapy for ongoing loss
Scalp micropigmentation

what: Rhinoplasty reshapes the bone and cartilage framework of the nose. In an open approach the surgeon makes a small incision across the columella, the strip of skin between the nostrils, and lifts the skin to work under direct vision. A closed approach keeps all incisions inside the nostrils. Cartilage may be trimmed, repositioned or grafted, and the nasal bones may be narrowed or straightened.

Where breathing is also a problem, septoplasty or turbinate reduction is often carried out at the same time; this combination is usually described as septorhinoplasty. Surgery typically takes two to four hours under general anaesthetic, with one night in hospital in many protocols.
cosmetic-surgery/rhinoplasty.why: Patients seek rhinoplasty to change the shape, size, profile or symmetry of the nose, to correct a deformity after injury, or to improve nasal airflow. Functional and cosmetic goals often overlap, and the assessment should cover both.
suitable: Completed facial growth — commonly from around 16–17 in women and 17–18 in men
Stable general health and no uncontrolled bleeding disorder
Specific, discussable goals rather than a general wish to look different
Understanding that this is one of the most technically demanding facial operations
notsuitable: Body dysmorphic disorder or expectations that cannot be met surgically
Active nasal or sinus infection at the time of surgery
Ongoing cocaine use or heavy smoking, both of which impair healing
Uncontrolled conditions that make general anaesthesia unsafe
Insufficient time to allow at least 12 months before judging the result
recovery: Days 1–7: splint or cast in place; swelling and bruising around the eyes peak at 48–72 hours
Around day 7: splint and any external sutures removed
Weeks 2–3: most people are back at desk work and socially presentable
Weeks 3–6: no contact sport, heavy lifting or glasses resting on the bridge unless the surgeon allows it
Months 3–12: fine swelling settles gradually, particularly at the tip
Final result usually judged at 12 months, longer for thick skin or revision cases
risks: Persistent or new breathing difficulty
Asymmetry, irregularity or a result that does not match what was planned
Revision surgery, which is needed in a meaningful minority of cases
Bleeding, infection, or septal perforation
Numbness of the nasal tip, usually temporary
Scarring at the columella in open approaches
Anaesthetic risks, including thrombosis
alternatives: Non-surgical rhinoplasty with dermal filler, for limited contour changes and with its own vascular risks
Septoplasty or turbinate reduction alone where the concern is purely functional
Camouflage with make-up or hairstyling
No treatment

what: Liposuction removes localised fat deposits through small incisions using a cannula connected to suction. Tumescent fluid containing local anaesthetic and adrenaline is infiltrated first to reduce bleeding and ease fat removal. Variants add ultrasound, laser or power assistance, but the underlying principle is the same.

It is a contouring operation, not a weight-loss operation. There is a safe ceiling on how much fat can be removed in one session — many surgeons work to around five litres of aspirate as a threshold beyond which risk rises sharply and inpatient monitoring is expected. Compression garments are worn for several weeks afterwards.
cosmetic-surgery/liposuction.why: Liposuction is considered for disproportionate fat deposits that persist despite stable weight and consistent exercise — flanks, abdomen, thighs, arms, back, under the chin. It does not treat obesity, loose skin or cellulite.
suitable: Stable weight close to a healthy range, with localised rather than generalised fat
Good skin elasticity, so the skin redrapes after volume is removed
Non-smoker or willing to stop well before surgery
Understanding that remaining fat cells still respond to weight gain
notsuitable: Using surgery as a weight-loss method
Significant skin laxity, where excision surgery gives a better result
Uncontrolled diabetes, cardiovascular disease or bleeding disorders
History of thrombosis without a managed prophylaxis plan
Multiple large-volume areas combined in a single session against the surgeon's advice
recovery: Days 1–3: soreness, bruising and fluid leakage from incision sites
Compression garment worn continuously for roughly 2–6 weeks as directed
Desk work usually resumes within 3–7 days depending on the areas treated
Exercise reintroduced from around weeks 3–4 with surgical approval
Swelling settles over 3–6 months; final contour typically judged at around 6 months
Manual lymphatic drainage is often recommended, though evidence for it varies
risks: Contour irregularity, rippling, asymmetry or over-resection
Seroma or haematoma formation
Prolonged swelling and altered sensation
Infection, and rarely necrotising soft-tissue infection
Fat embolism and venous thromboembolism — uncommon but serious
Fluid shifts and lidocaine toxicity in large-volume cases
Skin laxity becoming more apparent once volume is removed
alternatives: Supervised diet and exercise for generalised weight reduction
Non-invasive fat reduction such as cryolipolysis, with more modest effects
Abdominoplasty or body-lift surgery where loose skin is the main issue
No treatment

glance.Anaesthesia: General or tumescent local with sedation

what: Sleeve gastrectomy removes roughly 75–80% of the stomach laparoscopically, leaving a narrow tube — the sleeve — running from the oesophagus to the duodenum. The section removed includes most of the fundus, which produces much of the body's ghrelin, so the operation reduces both capacity and appetite signalling. It is not reversible.

Surgery takes about one to two hours under general anaesthetic through several small incisions, with a hospital stay commonly of two to three nights. It is the most frequently performed bariatric operation worldwide, but it is one component of a long-term programme that includes dietary change, supplementation and follow-up — not a standalone event.
bariatric-surgery/sleeve-gastrectomy.why: It is considered for people with obesity where supervised non-surgical measures have not achieved durable results, particularly where obesity-related conditions such as type 2 diabetes, sleep apnoea, hypertension or joint disease are present. Eligibility thresholds vary by country and by clinic.
suitable: Meeting the clinic's BMI and comorbidity criteria after full assessment
Completion of a multidisciplinary work-up including dietetic and psychological review
Commitment to lifelong dietary change, vitamin and mineral supplementation, and follow-up bloods
Fitness for laparoscopic surgery under general anaesthesia
notsuitable: Severe or poorly controlled gastro-oesophageal reflux, or Barrett's oesophagus — bypass is often preferred
Untreated eating disorder, active substance misuse or unstable mental health
Inability or unwillingness to attend long-term follow-up and take supplements
Pregnancy, or planned pregnancy within roughly 12–18 months of surgery
Medical conditions that make general anaesthesia or pneumoperitoneum unsafe
recovery: Hospital stay commonly 2–3 nights, with a leak test before discharge in many protocols
Staged diet: clear fluids, then full fluids, purée, soft food and finally normal textures over roughly 6–8 weeks under dietetic supervision
Desk work usually resumes at 2–4 weeks; heavy lifting avoided for around 6 weeks
Most weight loss occurs over the first 12–18 months
Lifelong supplementation and at least annual blood monitoring
Air travel is usually deferred until the clinic confirms it, commonly around 10–14 days, with thrombosis precautions
risks: Staple-line leak — uncommon but the most serious early complication, and one that typically presents after international patients have flown home
Bleeding, and venous thromboembolism
Stricture or narrowing of the sleeve
New or worsened reflux, sometimes requiring conversion to a bypass
Nutritional deficiencies including iron, vitamin B12, vitamin D and folate
Gallstones during rapid weight loss
Weight regain or insufficient weight loss
Loose skin that may prompt further surgery
alternatives: Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, often preferred where reflux is significant
One-anastomosis gastric bypass
Endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty or intragastric balloon, which are less invasive and generally less durable
Medical weight management including GLP-1 receptor agonists, under supervision
Structured lifestyle and dietetic programmes

what: Roux-en-Y gastric bypass creates a small stomach pouch, then joins it directly to a limb of small intestine, bypassing the rest of the stomach and the duodenum. A second connection further down returns digestive juices to the food stream, forming the Y shape the operation is named for. It restricts intake, alters gut hormone signalling and reduces absorption of some nutrients.

The operation is performed laparoscopically in most centres, takes roughly two to three hours, and usually involves a hospital stay of two to three nights. It has the longest track record of the mainstream bariatric procedures and is frequently the option chosen where reflux or type 2 diabetes is prominent.
bariatric-surgery/roux-en-y-gastric-bypa.why: It is considered for the same population as sleeve gastrectomy, and is often favoured where there is significant gastro-oesophageal reflux, hiatus hernia, or type 2 diabetes, where the metabolic effect tends to be more pronounced. It is also used as a revision after a sleeve.
suitable: Meeting the clinic's criteria after full multidisciplinary assessment
Significant reflux or Barrett's oesophagus, where a sleeve would be a poorer choice
Type 2 diabetes where a stronger metabolic effect is the goal
Willingness to commit to lifelong supplementation and monitoring
notsuitable: Inability to maintain lifelong vitamin and mineral supplementation
Untreated eating disorder or active substance misuse
Complex prior abdominal surgery making the anatomy hazardous, on the surgeon's judgement
Crohn's disease affecting the small bowel
Long-term need for medicines whose absorption would be unpredictable, without a management plan
recovery: Hospital stay commonly 2–3 nights
Staged diet from fluids to normal textures over roughly 6–8 weeks with dietetic supervision
Desk work usually at 2–4 weeks; heavy lifting avoided for around 6 weeks
Most weight loss over the first 12–18 months
Lifelong supplementation — including B12, iron, calcium and fat-soluble vitamins — with at least annual bloods
Air travel deferred until the clinic confirms, with thrombosis precautions
risks: Anastomotic leak — the most serious early complication
Internal hernia and bowel obstruction, which can occur years later and needs urgent assessment
Marginal ulcer, with a markedly higher risk in smokers and NSAID users
Dumping syndrome after sugary or high-fat meals
Nutritional deficiencies, more pronounced than after a sleeve
Bleeding, stricture and venous thromboembolism
Weight regain, gallstones and loose skin
Altered absorption of alcohol and of some medicines
alternatives: Sleeve gastrectomy
One-anastomosis gastric bypass
Endoscopic procedures or intragastric balloon
Medical weight management including GLP-1 receptor agonists
Structured lifestyle and dietetic programmes

what: LASIK corrects short-sightedness, long-sightedness and astigmatism by reshaping the cornea. A thin hinged flap is created — with a femtosecond laser in most modern practice — then lifted so an excimer laser can remove a precise amount of tissue underneath. The flap is repositioned and seals without stitches.

The laser treatment itself takes well under a minute per eye; both eyes are usually treated in one visit lasting around 20 to 30 minutes in total. Topical anaesthetic drops are used rather than a general anaesthetic. Vision is typically functional within a day, which is why LASIK is chosen over surface treatments by patients who need to return to work quickly.
eye-care/lasik.why: People choose LASIK to reduce dependence on glasses or contact lenses. It corrects refractive error; it does not prevent age-related presbyopia, and most patients will still need reading glasses from their mid-forties onwards.
suitable: Adults, typically 18 or older, with a stable prescription for at least 12 months
Adequate corneal thickness and a normal corneal topography
Refractive error within the range the clinic treats
Healthy eyes with no active disease, and realistic expectations about night vision and reading glasses
notsuitable: Keratoconus or suspicious corneal topography — a critical exclusion
Thin corneas relative to the correction required
Significant dry eye disease
Uncontrolled autoimmune or connective tissue disease, poorly controlled diabetes
Pregnancy or breastfeeding, when the prescription can shift
Advanced cataract or glaucoma, or an unstable prescription
recovery: First few hours: burning, watering and light sensitivity; rest with eyes closed
Day 1: most patients see well enough for everyday tasks and attend a next-day check
Week 1: no rubbing, swimming or eye make-up; protective shields often worn at night
Weeks 2–4: exercise and swimming reintroduced as directed
Dry eye and night-time halos are common early and usually settle over 3–6 months
Return travel is normally possible within a few days, but the day-one review should happen before flying
risks: Dry eye, occasionally persistent
Glare, halos and starbursts around lights at night
Under-correction or over-correction, sometimes requiring an enhancement
Flap complications: displacement, striae, or epithelial ingrowth
Infection or inflammation under the flap
Corneal ectasia — rare, serious, progressive weakening
Loss of some best-corrected vision in a small number of cases
alternatives: PRK or other surface ablation, which avoids a flap and suits thinner corneas
SMILE, a flapless intrastromal technique
Implantable collamer lens for high prescriptions or thin corneas
Refractive lens exchange, more often considered from middle age
Continuing with glasses or contact lenses

glance.Return-travel window: After the day-one review, confirmed by the clinic

what: Cataract surgery removes the eye's clouded natural lens and replaces it with a clear artificial intraocular lens. The standard technique, phacoemulsification, uses ultrasound through an incision of around 2–3 mm to break up the lens and aspirate it; the folded implant is then inserted into the remaining capsule, and the incision usually seals without stitches.

Each eye takes roughly 15 to 30 minutes under local anaesthetic, as a day case, with the second eye normally treated a week or more later. Lens choice matters as much as the surgery: a monofocal implant gives sharp vision at one distance, while multifocal, extended-depth-of-focus and toric options address a wider range at additional cost and with their own visual trade-offs.
eye-care/cataract-surgery.why: Surgery is considered when lens clouding blurs vision, causes glare or haloes, dulls colours or affects driving, reading and daily function. It is also performed to enable treatment or monitoring of other eye disease. It is the most commonly performed operation in many health systems.
suitable: Vision affected by cataract to a degree that interferes with daily life
Realistic expectations, particularly about premium lens options
Able to lie reasonably flat and cooperate for the duration
Any co-existing eye disease assessed beforehand, since it limits the achievable result
notsuitable: No functional impairment yet, where monitoring is reasonable
Active ocular infection or inflammation until treated
Advanced macular or optic nerve disease that would cap visual improvement — surgery may still be offered, with expectations set accordingly
Inability to attend post-operative review and use drops as prescribed
recovery: Vision often improves within days, though it may be blurred or gritty at first
Anti-inflammatory and antibiotic drops for roughly 2–4 weeks on a tapering schedule
No rubbing, swimming or heavy lifting for around two weeks
A shield worn at night for the first week in many protocols
Final glasses prescription usually settled at 4–6 weeks
The next-day and one-week checks should be arranged before any return travel
risks: Posterior capsule opacification — common, and treated with a quick YAG laser procedure
Endophthalmitis — rare but sight-threatening infection
Posterior capsule rupture or dropped lens fragments during surgery
Cystoid macular oedema
Retinal detachment, with higher risk in short-sighted eyes
Refractive surprise, so glasses are still needed
Raised intraocular pressure, corneal swelling, or dysphotopsia — unwanted glare and shadows
alternatives: Updated glasses and brighter task lighting while the cataract is mild
Delaying surgery and monitoring
Refractive lens exchange, which is the same operation performed before a cataract has developed

glance.Second eye: Usually a week or more later

what: Total knee replacement resurfaces the worn ends of the femur and tibia with metal components and inserts a plastic bearing between them; the back of the kneecap is resurfaced in some cases. The aim is to relieve pain from end-stage arthritis and restore functional movement, not to recreate a normal knee.

Surgery takes roughly one to two hours under spinal or general anaesthetic. Most centres now mobilise patients on the day of surgery, with a hospital stay of two to four nights. Rehabilitation, not the operation, determines most of the outcome — and it runs for months, which is the central planning problem for anyone having this done abroad.
orthopedics/total-knee-replacement.why: It is considered for advanced osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis or post-traumatic arthritis where pain disturbs sleep and daily activity and non-surgical measures — weight management, physiotherapy, analgesia, injections — no longer control symptoms.
suitable: Radiographic end-stage arthritis matching the reported symptoms
Non-surgical treatment already tried without adequate relief
Fit for anaesthesia and for an active rehabilitation programme
A realistic plan for supervised physiotherapy after returning home
notsuitable: Active infection anywhere in the body, particularly in or near the joint
Inadequate bone stock or a non-functioning extensor mechanism
Poorly controlled diabetes, or a body weight that substantially raises complication and revision risk
Smoking, until stopped, because of wound-healing and infection risk
No access to structured rehabilitation after discharge
recovery: Day 0–1: standing and walking with aids, usually the same day
Hospital stay commonly 2–4 nights
Weeks 1–6: daily physiotherapy; walking aids gradually reduced; range of motion is the priority
Weeks 6–12: most people walk without aids and return to desk work
Months 3–12: continued gains in strength and stamina; final outcome typically judged at 12 months
Air travel is high-risk for thrombosis after lower-limb surgery — the clinic should confirm timing and prophylaxis explicitly, commonly deferring flights for several weeks
risks: Venous thromboembolism — deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, a particular concern with long-haul travel
Prosthetic joint infection, which may require further surgery
Persistent pain or stiffness, and dissatisfaction despite technically sound surgery
Loosening or wear of components over time, leading to revision
Nerve or vessel injury, periprosthetic fracture
Manipulation under anaesthesia if the knee stiffens
Ongoing numbness around the scar
alternatives: Weight management, physiotherapy and structured exercise
Analgesia, including topical and oral options
Intra-articular corticosteroid injections
Partial or unicompartmental knee replacement where only one compartment is affected
Osteotomy in selected younger patients
Continuing with non-surgical management

what: Septoplasty straightens a deviated nasal septum — the partition of bone and cartilage between the nostrils. The surgeon works through incisions inside the nose, lifting the lining, then removing or repositioning the deviated portions before laying the lining back down. There is no external incision and no change to the outward shape of the nose.

It takes roughly 30 to 90 minutes, usually under general anaesthetic, and is commonly a day case or one overnight stay. Turbinate reduction is often performed at the same time, since enlarged turbinates frequently contribute to the blockage. If the external shape is also to be changed, the operation becomes a septorhinoplasty and is planned differently.
ent/septoplasty.why: It is offered for persistent nasal obstruction from a deviated septum that has not responded to medical treatment — typically one-sided blockage, mouth breathing, disturbed sleep, recurrent sinus infections or nosebleeds from a septal spur.
suitable: Symptomatic obstruction confirmed on examination to match the deviation
Medical treatment such as nasal steroids already tried
Completed facial growth in most protocols
Fit for general anaesthesia
notsuitable: Blockage caused mainly by allergy, polyps or rhinitis, which medical treatment should address first
Active nasal or sinus infection until treated
Uncontrolled bleeding disorder or anticoagulation without a management plan
Expectation that the operation will change the appearance of the nose — it will not
recovery: Days 1–3: congestion, mild bleeding and headache are usual; the nose feels more blocked before it feels better
Splints or dissolvable packing removed at around 5–7 days if used
Saline irrigation for several weeks as directed
Desk work usually at 1–2 weeks; no heavy lifting or nose-blowing for around 2 weeks
Breathing typically improves noticeably from weeks 2–6 as swelling settles
Flying is usually deferred until the clinic confirms, commonly around 1–2 weeks
risks: Persistent or recurrent obstruction, sometimes needing revision
Septal perforation
Bleeding, infection, or septal haematoma
Change in the shape of the nose, including a saddle deformity — uncommon
Reduced sense of smell
Numbness of the upper teeth or nasal tip, usually temporary
Adhesions between the septum and the lateral nasal wall
alternatives: Nasal corticosteroid sprays, antihistamines and saline irrigation
Turbinate reduction alone
Treatment of allergy or sinus disease
Nasal dilator strips for symptomatic relief
No treatment where symptoms are tolerable

what: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy removes the gallbladder through four small incisions. The abdomen is inflated with carbon dioxide, a camera and instruments are introduced, the cystic duct and artery are clipped and divided, and the gallbladder is separated from the liver bed and withdrawn. An intraoperative cholangiogram may be performed to check the bile ducts.

The operation takes roughly 45 to 90 minutes under general anaesthetic and is a day case or single overnight stay in most centres. A small proportion of operations are converted to an open procedure when inflammation or anatomy makes the laparoscopic view unsafe — that is a judgement in favour of safety, not a complication.
general-surgery/laparoscopic-cholecystec.why: It is performed for symptomatic gallstones — biliary colic, cholecystitis, gallstone pancreatitis — and for gallbladder polyps or dysfunction meeting the clinic's criteria. Gallstones found incidentally without symptoms are usually monitored rather than operated on.
suitable: Symptoms clearly attributable to the gallbladder, supported by imaging
Fit for general anaesthesia and pneumoperitoneum
No unresolved bile duct stones, or a plan to address them
Able to attend follow-up and seek care promptly if unwell after discharge
notsuitable: Asymptomatic gallstones in most cases
Suspected gallbladder cancer, which needs a different operation and pathway
Uncorrected coagulopathy
Late pregnancy, in most protocols
Severe cardiorespiratory disease making pneumoperitoneum unsafe
recovery: Day case or one night in hospital for most patients
Shoulder-tip pain from residual gas is common for a few days
Desk work usually resumes at 1–2 weeks; heavy lifting avoided for around 4 weeks
Wound care and suture or dressing removal as directed
Some people experience looser stools or fat intolerance for weeks to months
Flying is usually deferred until the clinic confirms, commonly around 7–10 days
risks: Bile duct injury — uncommon but the most serious complication, sometimes needing major reconstructive surgery
Bile leak, requiring drainage or endoscopic treatment
Retained stone in the common bile duct, presenting after discharge with jaundice or pain
Bleeding, wound infection, port-site hernia
Injury to bowel or blood vessels during access
Conversion to open surgery, with a longer recovery
Persistent symptoms afterwards, where the gallbladder was not the cause
alternatives: Dietary modification and analgesia for infrequent mild symptoms
Ursodeoxycholic acid in selected cases, with limited effectiveness
ERCP for duct stones, which does not treat the gallbladder itself
Percutaneous cholecystostomy in patients too unwell for surgery
Watchful waiting for asymptomatic stones

glance.Return-travel window: Often around 7–10 days, confirmed by the clinic
